newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian analysts dismiss Bhutto's remarks.
newsitem.headline: Indian analysts dismiss Bhutto's remarks.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto was trying to deflect attention from her troubles at home with remarks that New Delhi was bent on deploying nuclear-capable missiles, Indian political analysts said.
"It is a superfluous statement," said Sridhar, a senior official of the government-funded Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses.
Bhutto said on Wednesday that the world could not "remain indifferent to the rise of a fundamentalist Hindu India bent on producing and deploying nuclear capable ballistic missiles".
She was speaking at a meeting of foreign ministers of the 53-member Organisation of the Islamic Conference in New York.
"India's pursuit of a nuclear and ballistic weapons programme is of serious concern," she said.
"Of equal concern is its reluctance to engage in a meaningful dialogue on the issues of nuclear and conventional arms control bilaterally, regionally or globally."
New Delhi had no official reaction to Bhutto's statement, but one official who asked not to be named called her comments "desperate words" to deflect attention from Pakistan's own domestic tensions.
Pakistan has recently experienced political clashes and bombings. The violence peaked last month when Bhutto's brother Murtaza was killed in gunfire between supporters and police.

India exploded an atomic device in 1974 but says it has never built a nuclear bomb. Its longstanding stance has been to retain the option to build nuclear weapons. The government recently said it had no plans to test or build nuclear weapons.

Foreign Minister I.K. Gujral, attending the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York, was expected to react to Bhutto's statement, a Foreign Ministry official said. Analysts said they expected Gujral to make a low-key statement.
Former foreign secretary J.N. Dixit, who served as Indian high commissioner in Islamabad, said Bhutto was "talking through her hat".

Dixit said that on several occasions India had proposed the two neighbours sign an agreement vowing not to attack each other first with nuclear weapons. "Ms Bhutto has always rejected it outright," he said.
